prerequisites: Mathematical Methods from the first year
Mastery of thermometry and calorimetry concepts
Application of the first and second principles to closed systems and simple thermodynamic cycles

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing versatility to adapt to new situations
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, and critical reasoning
Ability to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills, and abilities in the field of Mechanical Engineering, both orally and in writing, and to all types of audiences
Knowledge for performing measurements, calculations, valuations, appraisals, expert reports, studies, reports, work plans, and other similar tasks
Ability to analyze and assess the social and environmental impact of technical solutions
Ability for occupational risk prevention and protection of workers' and users' health and safety
Honesty, responsibility, ethical commitment, and solidarity spirit
Ability to work in a team
Acquire knowledge of applied thermodynamics and heat transfer: Basic principles and their application to solving engineering problems
Relate the field of study of Thermodynamics and Heat Transfer and know the most important applications of both disciplines in the field of Thermal Engineering
Apply mass, energy, and entropy balances to various systems, including the main equipment present in industrial plants (engines, turbines, compressors, boilers, condensers, etc.)

Know the equipment that integrates power production cycles (steam, gas, and combined) and refrigeration cycles commonly used in industry and be able to perform their thermodynamic analysis to assess their energy efficiency
Know the main characteristics and fundamental physical laws on which the three basic mechanisms of heat transfer are based (conduction, convection, and radiation)
Mathematically express the equations that describe heat transfer in a physical problem from fundamental balances (mass, momentum, and heat) and the laws on which the basic mechanisms are based

syllabus_topics: BLOCK I. APPLIED THERMODYNAMICS
Chapter 1. Properties and Processes in Thermodynamic Systems

Lesson 1: Basic concepts: Units of measurement. Gases: ideal, real and Van der Waals. Equations of state. Pure substance: phases and diagrams. State properties: determination by using tables and/or equations of state.
Chapter 2. Basic Principles of Thermodynamics
Lesson 2. First Principle of Thermodynamics. Sign criterion. Application to closed and open systems in steady state.
Lesson 3. Second Principle of Thermodynamics. Entropy definition and applications. Entropy generation. Isentropic efficiency of equipment.
Chapter 3. Thermal Machines
Lesson 4. The thermal engine: types and efficiency. The Carnot cycle: thermal efficiency. Thermal engine cycles operating as motors: thermal efficiency.
Lesson 5. Gas power cycles: Brayton cycle analysis.
Lesson 6. Steam power cycles: Rankine cycle analysis. Combined cycle.
Lesson 7. Continuous cold production by vapor compression of a refrigerant: analysis of the inverse Rankine cycle. The heat pump and its analysis.
BLOCK II. BASIC CONCEPTS OF HEAT TRANSFER
Chapter 4. Fundamentals of heat transfer
Lesson 8: Fundamental concepts, characteristics of basic heat transfer mechanisms and basic laws.
Chapter 5. Conduction
Lesson 9. Simple geometries: plane, cylindrical and spherical wall. Critical insulation radius.
Lesson 10. Additional surfaces: concept, temperature field, efficiency and dissipation coefficient. Heat transfer through finned surfaces.
Lesson 11. Heat transfer in common configurations: shape factor in conduction.
Chapter 6. Convection
Lesson 12. Analysis methods in forced and natural convection.
Lesson 13. Use of empirical correlations in forced and natural convection.
Chapter 7. Radiation
Lesson 14. Fundamentals of thermal radiation. Radiative properties. Black body and gray body. Heat transfer by radiation between two surfaces. Combined heat transfer mechanisms.
teaching_methods: Virtual Campus activities (reading theoretical foundations, solving questionnaires, participating in debate forums, viewing additional material)
assessment_rules: For students with continuous evaluation, the course grade is calculated as (0.1 x PA) + (0.1 x PL) + (0.1 x TG) + (0.7 x EX), provided the written exam (EX) is 3.5 or higher. Otherwise, the grade will be the minimum of the calculated score and 4.0. A final course grade of 5.0 or higher is required to pass. For students with differentiated evaluation, the course grade is calculated as (0.3 x EP) + (0.7 x EX), provided the written exam (EX) is 3.5 or higher. Otherwise, the grade will be the minimum of the calculated score and 4.0. In extraordinary calls, a minimum of 3.5 in the written exam (EX) is required to pass, and for continuous evaluation students, the PA, PL, and TG grades from continuous evaluation are used in the same formula. For differentiated evaluation students in extraordinary calls, both a written exam (EX) and a practice exam (EP) are conducted, and the same formula and minimum grade rule apply. Students may choose to examine only one part of the subject (Block I or Block II) in the extraordinary written exam, using previous scores for the unexamined block if they meet the minimum.
